extraction_notes.note: The 'Remarks' environment 1.2 mainly defines 'diffusion process' (used by Definition 1.1), so it was typed as a definition. It also states the usual-conditions convention.
Theorem 1.5 is the paper's star-graph analogue of Feller's theorem. The paper proves it only by reference (Knight's proof adapted, or BMMG Thm 1.3), so it is marked external.

Generator and resolvent derivations in running text interleave lemmas with their proofs. Each was extracted as one prose proof that contains those lemmas as setup steps (step rule 10). Where they end follows the 'we have proved the following theorem' / 'another proof' sentences.

Results stated inside prose proofs are used again outside them: Dynkin's formula (TP7) in the proofs of Theorems 3.2 and 4.2, Lemma 2.1 in PP15/PP23, Lemma 3.3 in PP31, Corollary 4.6 in ClP29. These edges were kept because the paper really applies those results.
The pathwise construction of the Walsh process (zero set Z, excursion intervals, edge labels R_j, weights w_k) is kept as one definition node, not split per introduced symbol.
The two inverse Laplace transforms (3.7), (3.8) taken from the Erdelyi tables are kept as top-level equation nodes. They were not promoted to external theorems.

Short connective assertions such as 'Thus as above we get X(zeta_beta)=v', 'F^s_inf is contained in F^w_inf' and the parenthetical remark that the Dirichlet process is not a Brownian motion were left inside the surrounding text, not made into nodes.

nodes.name: Star graph
nodes.statement: The simplest metric graphs are \emph{star} or \emph{single vertex graphs}: They can be defined as a set having a finite collection of subsets isomorphic to $\mathbb{R}_+$, called \emph{external edges}, where the points corresponding to the origin of $\mathbb{R}_+$ under these isomorphims are identified and form the \emph{vertex} of the graph.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction and Preliminaries
nodes.genus: a set having a finite collection of subsets isomorphic to $\mathbb{R}_+$

nodes.name: Fixed star graph G
nodes.statement: From now we shall consider a fixed star graph $\mathcal{G}$ with vertex $v$ and $n\in\mathbb{N}$ external edges $l_1$, \dots, $l_n$.
nodes.section: 1.1 Brownian on a Star Graph and Feller's Theorem

nodes.name: Natural metric d on G
nodes.statement: $\mathcal{G}$ is equipped with the natural metric $d$ which is induced by the metric that each external edge inherits from being isomorphic to $\mathbb{R}_+$.
nodes.section: 1.1 Brownian on a Star Graph and Feller's Theorem

nodes.name: Open interior of G
nodes.statement: $\mathcal{G}^\circ$ denotes the set $\mathcal{G}\setminus\{v\}$ which we also call --- by abuse of language --- the \emph{open interior} of $\mathcal{G}$.
nodes.section: 1.1 Brownian on a Star Graph and Feller's Theorem

nodes.name: Open edges l_k^circ
nodes.statement: It is the disjoint union of $n$ copies $l_k^\circ$, $k=1$, \dots, $n$, of the interval $(0,+\infty)$.
nodes.section: 1.1 Brownian on a Star Graph and Feller's Theorem

nodes.name: Local coordinates
nodes.statement: Every $\xi\in\mathcal{G}^\circ$ is in one-to-one correspondence with its \emph{local coordinates} $(k,x)$, where $k\in\{1,\dotsc,n\}$ is the index of the edge $\xi$ belongs to, and $x>0$ denotes the distance of $\xi$ to $v$.
nodes.section: 1.1 Brownian on a Star Graph and Feller's Theorem

nodes.name: Notation xi=(k,x)
nodes.statement: For simplicity we shall often write $\xi=(k,x)$.
nodes.section: 1.1 Brownian on a Star Graph and Feller's Theorem

nodes.name: Brownian motion on a star graph
nodes.statement: A \emph{Brownian motion} $X=(X_t,\,t\in\mathbb{R}_+)$ on $\mathcal{G}$ is a diffusion process on $\mathcal{G}$, such that $X$ with absorption at $v$ is equivalent to a Brownian motion on the half line $\mathbb{R}_+$ with absorption at the origin.
nodes.section: 1.1 Brownian on a Star Graph and Feller's Theorem
differentia: $X$ with absorption at $v$ is equivalent to a Brownian motion on the half line $\mathbb{R}_+$ with absorption at the origin
nodes.label: def_BM

nodes.name: Diffusion process (convention)
nodes.statement: By a diffusion process we mean a strong Markov process (e.g., in the sense of~\cite{BlGe68}), which a.s.\ has c\`adl\`ag paths and a.s.\ the paths are continuous on $[0,\zeta)$, where $\zeta$ is its lifetime. Moreover, in definition~\ref{def_BM} we have --- as we shall usually do without any danger of confusion --- identified the external leg $l_k$, $k=1$, \dots, $n$, on which the process starts with the corresponding copy of $\mathbb{R}_+$. Throughout we shall assume without loss of generality that the filtration of a Brownian motion on $\mathcal{G}$ satisfies the ``usual conditions'', i.e., it is right continuous and complete relative to the underlying family $(P_\xi,\,\xi\in\mathcal{G})$ of probability measures.
nodes.section: 1.1 Brownian on a Star Graph and Feller's Theorem
differentia: a.s.\ has c\`adl\`ag paths and a.s.\ the paths are continuous on $[0,\zeta)$
nodes.label: rem_BM

nodes.name: Space C_0(G)
nodes.statement: $\ensuremath C_0(\mathcal{G})$ denotes the Banach space of continuous functions on $\mathcal{G}$ which vanish at infinity equipped with the sup-norm.
nodes.section: 1.1 Brownian on a Star Graph and Feller's Theorem
nodes.genus: Banach space of continuous functions on $\mathcal{G}$

nodes.name: Space C_0^2(G)
nodes.statement: Define $\ensuremath C_0^2(\mathcal{G})$ as the subspace of $\ensuremath C_0(\mathcal{G})$ consisting of those functions $f\in\ensuremath C_0(\mathcal{G})$ which are twice continuously differentiable on $\ensuremath\mathcal{G}\ensuremath^\circ$, such that $f''$ extends from $\mathcal{G}^\circ$ to $\mathcal{G}$ as a function in $\ensuremath C_0(\mathcal{G})$.
nodes.section: 1.1 Brownian on a Star Graph and Feller's Theorem
differentia: $f''$ extends from $\mathcal{G}^\circ$ to $\mathcal{G}$ as a function in $\ensuremath C_0(\mathcal{G})$

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 1.3 (omitted)
nodes.statement: It can be proved with the help of applications of the fundamental theorem of calculus and the mean value theorem, and the proof is omitted here.
nodes.section: 1.1 Brownian on a Star Graph and Feller's Theorem
nodes.statement_short: Fundamental theorem of calculus and mean value theorem; details omitted.

nodes.name: Properties of functions in C_0^2(G)
nodes.statement: Suppose that $f\in\ensuremath C_0^2(\mathcal{G})$, $k\in\{1,\dotsc,n\}$. Then the limit of $f'(\xi)$ as $\xi$ converges to $v$ along the open edge $l_k^\circ$ exists. The directional derivatives $f^{(i)}(v_k)$, $i=1$, $2$, of first and second order of $f$ at the vertex $v$ in direction of the edge $l_k$ exist, and the equalities \begin{equation*} f^{(i)}(v_k) = \lim_{\xi\to v,\,\xi\in l_k^\circ} f^{(i)}(\xi),\qquad i=1,\,2, \end{equation*} hold true. Moreover, $f'$ vanishes at infinity.
nodes.section: 1.1 Brownian on a Star Graph and Feller's Theorem
conclusions: the limit of $f'(\xi)$ as $\xi$ converges to $v$ along the open edge $l_k^\circ$ exists
nodes.statement_short: Functions in $C_0^2(\mathcal{G})$ have one-sided first and second derivatives at the vertex along each edge, obtained as limits; $f'$ vanishes at infinity.
nodes.label: lemC02

nodes.name: Second derivative at the vertex is edge independent
nodes.statement: By definition we have that for every $f\in\ensuremath C_0^2(\mathcal{G})$ and all $j$, $k=1$, \dots, $n$, $f''(v_j) = f''(v_k)$, and henceforth we shall simply write $f''(v)$ for this quantity. On the other hand, in general $f'(v_j)\ne f'(v_k)$ for $j\ne k$.
nodes.section: 1.1 Brownian on a Star Graph and Feller's Theorem
nodes.label: remC02

nodes.name: Every Brownian motion on a star graph is Feller
nodes.statement: It is not hard to show that every Brownian motion on a star graph is a Feller process.
nodes.section: 1.1 Brownian on a Star Graph and Feller's Theorem
conclusions: every Brownian motion on a star graph is a Feller process

nodes.name: Proof sketch of the Feller property
nodes.statement: A convenient way to prove this is to show that its resolvent maps $C_0(\mathcal{G})$ into itself by arguments similar to those in~\cite[Section~3.6]{ItMc74}, and to observe that the path properties imply for all $\xi\in\mathcal{G}$, $f\in\ensuremath C_0(\mathcal{G})$, $P_t f(\xi)$ converges to $f(\xi)$ as $t$ decreases to $0$, where $(P_t,\,t\in\mathbb{R}_+)$ denotes the semigroup generated by the Brownian motion. Then one can use well-known arguments (for example, a complete proof can be found in~\cite{NFSG}) to conclude the Feller property in its usual form, e.g., \cite{ReYo91}.
nodes.section: 1.1 Brownian on a Star Graph and Feller's Theorem
nodes.statement_short: Show the resolvent preserves $C_0(\mathcal{G})$ and $P_tf\to f$ pointwise, then invoke the known equivalence with the Feller property.

nodes.name: Feller's theorem for star graphs
nodes.statement: Assume that $X$ is a Brownian motion on $\mathcal{G}$. Then there exist constants $a$, $b_k$, $c\in[0,1]$, $k=1$, \dots, $n$, with \begin{subequations} \begin{equation} a + c + \sum_{k=1}^n b_k = 1,\quad a\ne 1, \end{equation} such that the domain $\mathcal{D}(A)$ of the generator $A$ of $X$ in $\ensuremath C_0(\mathcal{G})$ consists exactly of those $f\in\ensuremath C_0^2(\mathcal{G})$ for which \begin{equation} a f(v) + \frac{c}{2}\,f''(v) = \sum_{k=1}^n b_k f'(v_k) \end{equation} \end{subequations} holds true. Moreover, for $f\in\mathcal{D}(A)$, $Af = 1/2 f''$.
nodes.section: 1.1 Brownian on a Star Graph and Feller's Theorem
nodes.origin_citation: Knight 1981, Thm 6.2; Kostrykin, Potthoff & Schrader (BMMG), Thm 1.3
conclusions: the domain $\mathcal{D}(A)$ of the generator $A$ of $X$ in $\ensuremath C_0(\mathcal{G})$ consists exactly of those $f\in\ensuremath C_0^2(\mathcal{G})$ for which
nodes.statement_short: The generator of any Brownian motion on a star graph is $\frac12 f''$ on $C_0^2$ functions satisfying a Wentzell-type vertex condition $af(v)+\frac c2 f''(v)=\sum b_k f'(v_k)$.
nodes.label: thm_Feller

nodes.name: Parameter normalization (1.1a)
nodes.statement: a + c + \sum_{k=1}^n b_k = 1,\quad a\ne 1,
nodes.section: 1.1 Brownian on a Star Graph and Feller's Theorem
nodes.label: eq1.1a

nodes.name: Boundary condition at the vertex (1.1b)
nodes.statement: a f(v) + \frac{c}{2}\,f''(v) = \sum_{k=1}^n b_k f'(v_k)
nodes.section: 1.1 Brownian on a Star Graph and Feller's Theorem
nodes.label: eq1.1b

nodes.name: Proof of Feller's theorem (by reference)
nodes.statement: The proof in~\cite{Kn81} for the case where $\mathcal{G}$ has only one external edge, i.e., $\mathcal{G}=\mathbb{R}_+$, is readily modified for a general star graph $\mathcal{G}$. On the other hand, theorem~\ref{thm_Feller} also follows from Feller's theorem in the case of a general metric graph~\cite[Theorem~1.3]{BMMG}.
nodes.section: 1.1 Brownian on a Star Graph and Feller's Theorem
nodes.statement_short: Adapt Knight's half-line proof, or specialize Feller's theorem for general metric graphs.

nodes.name: Standard Brownian motion B
nodes.statement: Let $(Q_x,\,x\in\mathbb{R})$ denote a family of probability measures on a measurable space $(\Omega',\mathcal{A}')$, and let $B=(B_t,\,t\in\mathbb{R}_+)$ denote a standard Brownian motion defined on $(\Omega',\mathcal{A}')$ with $Q_x(B_0=x)=1$, $x\in\mathbb{R}$.
nodes.section: 1.2 Standard Brownian Motion on the Real Line

nodes.name: B has continuous paths
nodes.statement: It will be convenient to assume throughout that $B$ exclusively has continuous paths.

nodes.name: Shift operator theta
nodes.statement: Furthermore, we may suppose that there is a shift operator $\theta: \mathbb{R}_+\times\Omega \to\Omega$, such that for all $s$, $t\ge 0$, $B_s\circ\theta_t=B_{s+t}$.
nodes.section: 1.2 Standard Brownian Motion on the Real Line

nodes.name: Filtration J
nodes.statement: We shall always understand the Brownian family $(B, (Q_x,\,x\in\mathbb{R}))$ to be equipped with a filtration $\mathcal{J}=(\mathcal{J}_t,\,t\ge 0)$ which is right continuous and complete for the family $(Q_x,\,x\in\mathbb{R})$.
nodes.section: 1.2 Standard Brownian Motion on the Real Line

nodes.name: Hitting time H^B_A
nodes.statement: For any $A\subset\mathbb{R}$, we denote by $H^B_A$ the hitting time of $A$ by $B$, \begin{equation} H^B_A = \inf\{t>0,\,B_t\in A\}, \end{equation} and we note that for all $A$ belonging to the Borel $\sigma$--algebra $\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})$ of $\mathbb{R}$, $H^B_A$ is a stopping time with respect to $\mathcal{J}$ (e.g., \cite[Theorem~III.2.17]{ReYo91}).

nodes.name: Notation H^B(A)

nodes.statement: Let $x\in\mathbb{R}$. Then we have (e.g., \cite[Sect.~1.7]{ItMc74}, \cite[Sect.~2.6]{KaSh91}, \cite[Sect.'s~II.3, III.3]{ReYo91}) \begin{equation} Q_0(H^B_x\in dt) = Q_x(H^B_0\in dt) = \frac{|x|}{t}\,g(t,x)\,dt,\qquad t>0, \end{equation} where $g$ is the Gau{\ss}-kernel \begin{equation} g(t,x) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi t}}\,e^{-x^2/2t},\qquad t>0,\,x\in\mathbb{R}, \end{equation} and \begin{equation} E^Q_0\bigl(e^{-\lambda H^B_x}\bigr) = E^Q_x\bigl(e^{-\lambda H^B_0}\bigr) = e^{-\ensuremath\sqrt{2\lambda} |x|},\qquad \lambda>0. \end{equation}

nodes.section: 1.4 \boldmath The Case $b=0$
nodes.statement_short: The exponential factor inverts to the hitting time density.

nodes.name: Laplace transform of the hitting time density
nodes.statement: \int_0^\infty e^{-\lambda s}\,\frac{a}{\sqrt{2\pi s^3}}\,e^{-a^2/2s}\,ds = e^{-\ensuremath\sqrt{2\lambda} a},\qquad a>0,\,\lambda>0,
nodes.section: 1.4 \boldmath The Case $b=0$

nodes.name: Heat kernel of the b=0 process
nodes.statement: Thus we obtain the following heat kernel \begin{equation} \begin{split} p^0(t,\xi,d\eta) &= p^D(t,\xi,\eta)\,d\eta - \Bigl(\int_0^t e^{-\beta(t-s)} \,P_\xi(H_v\in ds)\Bigr)\,\epsilon_v(d\eta),\\[1ex] &= p^D(t,\xi,\eta)\,d\eta - \Bigl(\int_0^t e^{-\beta(t-s)} \,\frac{d(\xi,v)}{\sqrt{2\pi s^3}}\,e^{-d(\xi,v)^2/2s}\,ds\Bigr)\,\epsilon_v(d\eta), \end{split} \end{equation} with $\xi$, $\eta\in\mathcal{G}$, $t>0$, and $\epsilon_v$ is the Dirac measure at the vertex $v$.
nodes.section: 1.4 \boldmath The Case $b=0$
nodes.statement_short: Transition kernel of the stopped-and-killed process: Dirichlet kernel plus a vertex atom weighted by the killed hitting time density.

nodes.name: Heat kernel of the process with b=0
nodes.statement: \begin{split} p^0(t,\xi,d\eta) &= p^D(t,\xi,\eta)\,d\eta - \Bigl(\int_0^t e^{-\beta(t-s)} \,P_\xi(H_v\in ds)\Bigr)\,\epsilon_v(d\eta),\\[1ex] &= p^D(t,\xi,\eta)\,d\eta - \Bigl(\int_0^t e^{-\beta(t-s)} \,\frac{d(\xi,v)}{\sqrt{2\pi s^3}}\,e^{-d(\xi,v)^2/2s}\,ds\Bigr)\,\epsilon_v(d\eta), \end{split}

nodes.name: Infinite lifetime and non-absorbing vertex
nodes.statement: In this subsection we suppose that $X$ is a Brownian motion on the single vertex graph $\mathcal{G}$ with infinite lifetime, and such that the vertex is not absorbing.
nodes.section: 1.5 Killing via the Local Time at the Vertex

nodes.name: The vertex is regular
nodes.statement: This entails (e.g., \cite[Proposition~II.2.19]{ReYo91}) that $X$ leaves the vertex immediately and begins a standard Brownian excursion into one of the edges. Therefore we get in this case for the hitting time $H_v$ of the vertex $P_v(H_v=0)=1$, i.e., $v$ is regular for $\{v\}$ in the sense of~\cite{BlGe68}.
nodes.section: 1.5 Killing via the Local Time at the Vertex
conclusions: $X$ leaves the vertex immediately and begins a standard Brownian excursion into one of the edges
$v$ is regular for $\{v\}$ in the sense of~\cite{BlGe68}

nodes.name: Local time L at the vertex
nodes.statement: Consequently $X$ has a local time $L=(L_t,\,t\ge 0)$ at the vertex (e.g., \cite[Theorem~V.3.13]{BlGe68}).
nodes.section: 1.5 Killing via the Local Time at the Vertex

nodes.name: L is a PCHAF
nodes.statement: Without loss of generality, we suppose throughout this subsection that $L$ is a \emph{perfect continuous homogeneous additive functional (PCHAF)} of $X$ in the sense of~\cite[Section~III.32]{Wi79}.
nodes.section: 1.5 Killing via the Local Time at the Vertex

nodes.name: Perfect continuous homogeneous additive functional (PCHAF)
nodes.statement: That is, $L$ is a non-decreasing process, which is adapted to $\mathcal{F}$, and such that it is a.s.\ continuous, additive, i.e., $L_{t+s} = L_t + L_s\circ \theta_t$, and for all $\xi\in\mathcal{G}$, $P_\xi\bigl(L_0=0\bigr)=1$ holds true.
nodes.section: 1.5 Killing via the Local Time at the Vertex
nodes.genus: non-decreasing process, which is adapted to $\mathcal{F}$

nodes.name: X and L pathwise continuous
nodes.statement: Moreover we may and will assume from now on that $X$ and $L$ are \emph{pathwise} continuous.
nodes.section: 1.5 Killing via the Local Time at the Vertex

nodes.name: Pseudo-inverse K of L
nodes.statement: Let $K=(K_s,\,s\in\mathbb{R}_+)$ denote the right continuous pseudo-inverse of $L$: \begin{equation} K_s = \inf\{t\ge 0,\,L_t>s\},\qquad s\in\mathbb{R}_+, \end{equation} where --- as usual --- we make the convention that $\inf\emptyset=+\infty$.
nodes.section: 1.5 Killing via the Local Time at the Vertex

nodes.name: Right continuous pseudo-inverse K of L
nodes.statement: K_s = \inf\{t\ge 0,\,L_t>s\},\qquad s\in\mathbb{R}_+,
nodes.section: 1.5 Killing via the Local Time at the Vertex
nodes.label: eq_def_K

nodes.name: Basic properties of K
nodes.statement: The continuity of $L$ entails that for every $s\in\mathbb{R}_+$, $L_{K_s}=s$. Clearly, $K$ is increasing, and due to its right continuity it is a measurable stochastic process.
nodes.section: 1.5 Killing via the Local Time at the Vertex
conclusions: it is a measurable stochastic process

nodes.name: Identity {K_s<t}={L_t>s}
nodes.statement: Fix $s\in\mathbb{R}_+$. It is straightforward to check that for every $t\in\mathbb{R}_+$, \begin{equation} \{K_s < t\} = \{L_t > s\}. \end{equation}
nodes.section: 1.5 Killing via the Local Time at the Vertex

nodes.name: Identity {K_s<t}={L_t>s}
nodes.section: 1.5 Killing via the Local Time at the Vertex
nodes.label: eq_set_K

nodes.name: K_s is a stopping time
nodes.statement: Because $L$ is adapted, the set on the right hand side belongs to $\mathcal{F}_t$, and since $\mathcal{F}$ is right continuous, equality~\eqref{eq_set_K} shows that for every $s\in\mathbb{R}_+$, $K_s$ is a stopping time relative to $\mathcal{F}$.
nodes.section: 1.5 Killing via the Local Time at the Vertex
conclusions: for every $s\in\mathbb{R}_+$, $K_s$ is a stopping time relative to $\mathcal{F}$

nodes.name: X is at the vertex at times K_s
nodes.statement: We remark that since $L$ only increases when $X$ is at the vertex $v$, the continuity of $X$ implies that for every $s\in\mathbb{R}_+$ we get $X(K_s) = v$ on $\{K_s<+\infty\}$. On the other hand, we shall argue below that $L$ a.s.\ increases to $+\infty$, so that we get $X(K_s)=v$ a.s.\ for all $s\in\mathbb{R}_+$.
nodes.section: 1.5 Killing via the Local Time at the Vertex

nodes.name: Exponential law P_beta
nodes.statement: Let $\beta>0$. Bring in the additional probability space $(\mathbb{R}_+, \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}_+), P_\beta)$, where $P_\beta$ is the exponential law with rate $\beta$.
nodes.section: 1.5 Killing via the Local Time at the Vertex

nodes.name: Coordinate random variable S
nodes.statement: Let $S$ denote the associated coordinate random variable $S(s) = s$, $s\in\mathbb{R}_+$.
nodes.section: 1.5 Killing via the Local Time at the Vertex

nodes.name: Enlarged probability spaces
nodes.statement: Define \begin{equation*} \ensuremath{\hat\Omega} = \Omega\times\mathbb{R}_+,\quad \ensuremath{\hat {\mathcal{A}}} = \mathcal{A}\otimes\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}_+),\quad \ensuremath{\hat P}_\xi = P_\xi\otimes P_\beta,\ \xi\in\mathcal{G}. \end{equation*}
nodes.section: 1.5 Killing via the Local Time at the Vertex

nodes.name: Killing time zeta_beta
nodes.statement: Set \begin{equation} \zeta_\beta = \inf\bigl\{t\ge 0,\,L_t>S\bigr\}, \end{equation} and observe that since $K$ is measurable we may write $\zeta_\beta = K_S$.
nodes.section: 1.5 Killing via the Local Time at the Vertex

nodes.name: Killing time zeta_beta
nodes.statement: \zeta_\beta = \inf\bigl\{t\ge 0,\,L_t>S\bigr\},

nodes.label: eq1.28

nodes.name: Killed process
nodes.statement: Define the \emph{killed process} \begin{equation} \ensuremath{\hat X}_t = \begin{cases} X_t, & t<\zeta_\beta,\\ \Delta, & t\ge \zeta_\beta. \end{cases} \end{equation}
nodes.section: 1.5 Killing via the Local Time at the Vertex

nodes.name: Killed process
nodes.statement: \ensuremath{\hat X}_t = \begin{cases} X_t, & t<\zeta_\beta,\\ \Delta, & t\ge \zeta_\beta. \end{cases}

nodes.label: eq1.29

nodes.name: Killing via the local time preserves the strong Markov property
nodes.statement: However, it has been proved in~\cite[Appendix~A]{BMMG0} that the strong Markov property is preserved under this method of killing, i.e., $\ensuremath{\hat X}$ is a strong Markov process relative to its natural filtration (actually relative to a larger filtration, but we will not use this here).
nodes.section: 1.5 Killing via the Local Time at the Vertex
conclusions: $\ensuremath{\hat X}$ is a strong Markov process relative to its natural filtration

nodes.name: Killed process is strong Markov for the augmented filtration
nodes.statement: Now we may employ the arguments in section~2.7 of~\cite{KaSh91}, or in section~III.2 of~\cite{ReYo91} to conclude that $\ensuremath{\hat X}$ is a strong Markov process with respect to the universal right continuous and complete augmentation of its natural filtration.
nodes.section: 1.5 Killing via the Local Time at the Vertex
conclusions: $\ensuremath{\hat X}$ is a strong Markov process with respect to the universal right continuous and complete augmentation of its natural filtration

nodes.name: Proof that the killed process is a Brownian motion
nodes.statement: It is clear that $\ensuremath{\hat X}$ has a.s.\ right continuous paths which admit left limits, and that its paths on $[0,\zeta_\beta)$ are equal to those of $X$, and thus are continuous on this random time interval. Moreover, it is obvious that for every $\xi\in\ensuremath\mathcal{G}\ensuremath^\circ$, we have $P_\xi(\zeta_\beta \ge H_v)=1$. Therefore, up to its hitting time of the vertex, $\ensuremath{\hat X}$ is equivalent to a Brownian motion on the edge to which $\xi$ belongs, because so is $X$.
nodes.section: 1.5 Killing via the Local Time at the Vertex
nodes.statement_short: Paths agree with those of $X$ before $\zeta_\beta\ge H_v$, so up to $H_v$ the killed process is an edge Brownian motion.

nodes.name: Killed process is a Brownian motion on G
nodes.statement: Altogether we have proved that --- under the hypothesis that $L$ is a PCHAF, which will be argued below in all cases that we consider --- $\ensuremath{\hat X}$ is a Brownian motion on $\mathcal{G}$ in the sense of definition~\ref{def_BM}.
nodes.section: 1.5 Killing via the Local Time at the Vertex
assumptions: under the hypothesis that $L$ is a PCHAF
conclusions: $\ensuremath{\hat X}$ is a Brownian motion on $\mathcal{G}$ in the sense of definition~\ref{def_BM}

nodes.name: Resolvent of the killed process
nodes.statement: For all $\lambda>0$, $f\in B(\mathcal{G})$, $\xi\in\mathcal{G}$, \begin{equation} \ensuremath{\hat R}_\lambda f(\xi) = R_\lambda f(\xi) - e_\lambda(\xi)\,\ensuremath{\hat E}_v\bigl(e^{-\lambda \zeta_\beta}\bigr)\,R_\lambda f(v) \end{equation} holds true, where $e_\lambda$ is defined in equation~\eqref{eq1.14}.

conclusions: \ensuremath{\hat R}_\lambda f(\xi) = R_\lambda f(\xi) - e_\lambda(\xi)\,\ensuremath{\hat E}_v\bigl(e^{-\lambda \zeta_\beta}\bigr)\,R_\lambda f(v)

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 1.11
nodes.statement: For $\lambda>0$, $f\in B(\mathcal{G})$, $\xi\in\mathcal{G}$ \begin{align*} \ensuremath{\hat R}_\lambda f(\xi) &= \ensuremath{\hat E}_\xi\Bigl(\int_0^{\zeta_\beta} e^{-\lambda t} f(X_t)\,dt\Bigr)\\ &= R_\lambda f(\xi) - \ensuremath{\hat E}_\xi\Bigl(e^{-\lambda\zeta_\beta} \int_0^\infty e^{-\lambda t}\,f\bigl(X_{t+\zeta_\beta}\bigr)\,dt\Bigr). \end{align*} By construction, the last expectation value is equal to \begin{equation*} \beta\int_0^\infty e^{-\beta s}\int_0^\infty e^{-\lambda t} E_\xi\Bigl(e^{-\lambda K_s}\,f\bigl(X_{t+K_s}\bigr)\Bigr)\,dt\,ds, \end{equation*} where we used Fubini's theorem. Consider the expectation value under the integrals, and recall that for fixed $s\in\mathbb{R}_+$, $K_s$ is an $\mathcal{F}$--stopping time, while $X$ is strongly Markovian relative to $\mathcal{F}$. Hence we can compute as follows \begin{align*} E_\xi\Bigl(e^{-\lambda K_s}\,f\bigl(X_{t+K_s}\bigr)\Bigr) &= E_\xi\Bigl(e^{-\lambda K_s}\,E_\xi\Bigl(f\bigl(X_{t+K_s}\bigr)\ensuremath\,\big|\, \mathcal{F}_{K_s}\Bigr)\Bigr)\\ &= E_\xi\Bigl(e^{-\lambda K_s}\,E_{X(K_s)}\bigl(f(X_t)\bigr)\Bigr)\\ &= E_\xi\bigl(e^{-\lambda K_s}\bigr)\,E_v\bigl(f(X_t)\bigr), \end{align*} where we used the fact that a.s.\ $X(K_s)=v$. So far we have established \begin{equation*} \ensuremath{\hat R}_\lambda f(\xi) = R_\lambda f(\xi) - \ensuremath{\hat E}_\xi\bigl(e^{-\lambda \zeta_\beta}\bigr)\,R_\lambda f(v). \end{equation*} In order to compute the expectation value on the right hand side, we first remark that because $L$ is zero until $X$ hits the vertex for the first time, we find that for given $s\in\mathbb{R}_+$, $K_s\ge H_v$, and therefore $K_s = H_v + K_s\circ \theta_{H_v}$. Hence, and again by the strong Markov property, \begin{align*} E_\xi\bigl(e^{-\lambda K_s}\bigr) &= E_\xi\bigl(e^{-\lambda H_v}\,e^{-\lambda K_s\circ H_v}\bigr)\\ &= E_\xi\bigl(e^{-\lambda H_v}\,E_\xi\bigl(e^{-\lambda K_s\circ H_v}\ensuremath\,\big|\, \mathcal{F}_{H_v}\bigr)\bigr)\\ &= E_\xi\bigl(e^{-\lambda H_v}\bigr) E_v\bigl(e^{-\lambda K_s}\bigr), \end{align*} Integrating the last identity against the exponential law in the variable $s$, we find with formula~\eqref{eq1.14} \begin{equation*} \ensuremath{\hat E}_\xi\bigl(e^{-\lambda\zeta_\beta}\bigr) = e_\lambda(\xi)\,\ensuremath{\hat E}_v\bigl(e^{-\lambda \zeta_\beta}\bigr), \end{equation*} and the proof is finished.

nodes.statement_short: Split the resolvent integral at $\zeta_\beta=K_S$ and apply the strong Markov property at $K_s$ and at $H_v$. The key step is $X(K_s)=v$, so the post-killing part factors through $R_\lambda f(v)$.

nodes.name: Use the exponential law

nodes.name: Strong Markov at K_s
nodes.statement: Consider the expectation value under the integrals, and recall that for fixed $s\in\mathbb{R}_+$, $K_s$ is an $\mathcal{F}$--stopping time, while $X$ is strongly Markovian relative to $\mathcal{F}$. Hence we can compute as follows \begin{align*} E_\xi\Bigl(e^{-\lambda K_s}\,f\bigl(X_{t+K_s}\bigr)\Bigr) &= E_\xi\Bigl(e^{-\lambda K_s}\,E_\xi\Bigl(f\bigl(X_{t+K_s}\bigr)\ensuremath\,\big|\, \mathcal{F}_{K_s}\Bigr)\Bigr)\\ &= E_\xi\Bigl(e^{-\lambda K_s}\,E_{X(K_s)}\bigl(f(X_t)\bigr)\Bigr)\\ &= E_\xi\bigl(e^{-\lambda K_s}\bigr)\,E_v\bigl(f(X_t)\bigr), \end{align*} where we used the fact that a.s.\ $X(K_s)=v$. nodes.name: Strong Markov at H_v
nodes.statement: In order to compute the expectation value on the right hand side, we first remark that because $L$ is zero until $X$ hits the vertex for the first time, we find that for given $s\in\mathbb{R}_+$, $K_s\ge H_v$, and therefore $K_s = H_v + K_s\circ \theta_{H_v}$. Hence, and again by the strong Markov property, \begin{align*} E_\xi\bigl(e^{-\lambda K_s}\bigr) &= E_\xi\bigl(e^{-\lambda H_v}\,e^{-\lambda K_s\circ H_v}\bigr)\\ &= E_\xi\bigl(e^{-\lambda H_v}\,E_\xi\bigl(e^{-\lambda K_s\circ H_v}\ensuremath\,\big|\, \mathcal{F}_{H_v}\bigr)\bigr)\\ &= E_\xi\bigl(e^{-\lambda H_v}\bigr) E_v\bigl(e^{-\lambda K_s}\bigr), \end{align*} Integrating the last identity against the exponential law in the variable $s$, we find with formula~\eqref{eq1.14} \begin{equation*} \ensuremath{\hat E}_\xi\bigl(e^{-\lambda\zeta_\beta}\bigr) = e_\lambda(\xi)\,\ensuremath{\hat E}_v\bigl(e^{-\lambda \zeta_\beta}\bigr), \end{equation*} and the proof is finished.

nodes.statement: Formula~\eqref{eq1.30} is quite useful, because if the resolvent of $X$ is known, then --- in view of equation~\eqref{eq1.14} --- it reduces the calculation of $\ensuremath{\hat R}_\lambda$ to the computation of the Laplace transform of the density of $\zeta_\beta$ under $\ensuremath{\hat P}_v$.

nodes.name: Walsh process
nodes.statement: A pathwise construction of the Walsh process in the present context is as follows. Consider the paths of the standard Brownian motion $B=(B_t,\,t\ge 0)$ on $\mathbb{R}$, and its associated reflected Brownian motion $|B|=(|B_t|,\,t\ge 0)$, where $|\,\cdot\,|$ denotes absolute value. Let $Z=\{t\ge 0,\,B_t=0\}$. Then its complement $Z^c$ is open, and hence it is the pairwise disjoint union of a countable family of \emph{excursion intervals} $I_j = (t_j, t_{j+1})$, $j\in\mathbb{N}$. Let $R=(R_j,\,j\in\mathbb{N})$ be an independent sequence of identically distributed random variables, independent of $B$, with values in $\ensuremath\{1,2,\dotsc,n\}$ such that $R_j$, $j\in\mathbb{N}$, takes the value $k\in\ensuremath\{1,2,\dotsc,n\}$ with probability $w_k\in [0,1]$, $\sum_k w_k =1$. Now define $W_t = v$ if $t\in Z$, and if $t\in I_j$, and $R_j = k$ set $W_t = (k, |B_t|)$. In other words, when starting at $\xi\in\ensuremath\mathcal{G}\ensuremath^\circ$, the process moves as a Brownian motion on the edge containing $\xi$ until it hits the vertex at time $H_v$, and then $W$ performs Brownian excursions from the vertex $v$ into the edges $l_k$, $k\in\ensuremath\{1,2,\dotsc,n\}$, whereby the edge $l_k$ is selected with probability $w_k$.
nodes.section: 2 The Walsh Process
nodes.statement_short: Walsh process: reflected Brownian motion whose excursions from 0 are sent independently into edge $l_k$ with probability $w_k$.

nodes.name: W has continuous paths
nodes.statement: As for the standard Brownian motion on $\mathbb{R}$ (cf.\ subsection~\ref{ssect1.2}), we may and will assume without loss of generality that $W$ has exclusively continuous paths.
nodes.section: 2 The Walsh Process

nodes.name: Walsh process is strongly Markovian
nodes.statement: Walsh has remarked in the epilogue of~\cite{Wa78}, cf.\ also~\cite{BaPi89}, that it is not completely straightforward to prove that this stochastic process is strongly Markovian. A proof of the strong Markov property based on It\^o's excursion theory~\cite{It71a} has been given in~\cite{Sa86a, Sa86b}.

nodes.name: Derivation of the Walsh boundary condition (proof of Theorem 2.2)
nodes.statement: Next we check that the Walsh process has a generator with boundary condition at the vertex given by \eqref{eq1.1} with $a=c=0$. Let $f\in\mathcal{D}(A^w)$. At the vertex $v$ Dynkin's form for the generator reads \begin{equation} A^w f(v) = \lim_{\epsilon\ensuremath\downarrow 0} \frac{E_v\Bigl(f\bigl((X(\ensuremath H^w_{v,\epsilon})\bigr)\Bigr)-f(v)} {E_v(\ensuremath H^w_{v,\epsilon})}, \end{equation} where $\ensuremath H^w_{v,\epsilon}$ is the hitting time of the complement of the open ball $B_\epsilon(v)$ of radius $\epsilon>0$ around $v$. \begin{lemma} For the Walsh process $E_v(\ensuremath H^w_{v,\epsilon}) = \epsilon^2$. \end{lemma} \begin{proof} Since by construction $W$ has infinite lifetime, $\ensuremath H^w_{v,\epsilon}$ is the hitting time of the set of the $n$ points with local coordinates $(k,\epsilon)$, $\ensuremath k=1,\dotsc,n$. Therefore, by the independence of the choice of the edge for the values of the excursion, it follows that under $P_v$ the stopping time $\ensuremath H^w_{v,\epsilon}$ has the same law as the hitting time of the point $\epsilon>0$ of a reflected Brownian motion on $\mathbb{R}_+$, starting at $0$. Thus the statement of the lemma follows from equation~\eqref{eq1.6}. \end{proof} From the construction of $W$ we immediately get \begin{equation*} E_v\Bigl(f\bigl(W(\ensuremath H^w_{v,\epsilon})\bigr)\Bigr) = \sum_{k=1}^n w_k f_k(\epsilon), \end{equation*} with the notation $f_k(x)=f(k,x)$, $x\in\mathbb{R}_+$. Inserting this into equation~\eqref{eq2.1} we obtain \begin{equation*} A^w f(v) = \lim_{\epsilon\ensuremath\downarrow 0} \epsilon^{-2} \sum_{k=1}^n w_k \bigl(f_k(\epsilon)-f(v)\bigr), \end{equation*} and since $f'(v_k)$ exists (cf.\ lemma~\ref{lemC02}) it is obvious that this entails the condition \begin{equation} \sum_{k=1}^n w_k f'(v_k) = 0. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Scattering matrix of the Walsh process
nodes.statement: The matrix $\ensuremath S^w=\bigl(\ensuremath S^w_{km},\,k,m = 1,\dotsc,n\bigr)$ is the \emph{scattering matrix} as defined in quantum mechanics. We briefly recall its construction in the present context, for more details the interested reader is referred to~\cite{KoSc99}. $\ensuremath S^w$ is obtained from the boundary conditions at the vertex $v$ in the following way. Consider a function $f$ on $\mathcal{G}$ which is continuously differentiable in $\ensuremath\mathcal{G}\ensuremath^\circ=\mathcal{G}\setminus\{v\}$, and such that for all $\ensuremath k=1,\dotsc,n$ the limits \begin{align*} F_k &= f(v_k) = \lim_{\xi\to v,\,\xi\in l_k\ensuremath^\circ} f(\xi)\\ F'_k &= f'(v_k) = \lim_{\xi\to v,\,\xi\in l_k\ensuremath^\circ} f'(\xi) \end{align*} exist. Define two column vectors $F$, $F'\in\mathbb{C}^n$, having the components $F_k$ and $F'_k$, $\ensuremath k=1,\dotsc,n$, respectively. Furthermore, consider boundary conditions of the following form \begin{equation} A F + B F' =0, \end{equation} where $A$ and $B$ are complex $n\times n$ matrices. The \emph{on-shell scattering matrix at energy $E>0$} is defined as \begin{equation} S_{A,B}(E) = - (A+i\sqrt{E}B)^{-1}(A-i\sqrt{E}B), \end{equation} which exists and is unitary, provided the $n\times 2n$ matrix $(A,B)$ has maximal rank (i.e., rank $n$) and $AB^\dagger$ is hermitian. These requirements for $A$ and $B$ guarantee that the corresponding Laplace operator is self-adjoint on $L^2(\mathcal{G})$ (with Lebesgue measure). Observe that under these conditions the boundary conditions~\eqref{bc} are equivalent to any boundary conditions of the form $CAF+CBF'=0$ where $C$ is invertible. Also $S_{CA, CB}(E) = S_{A,B}(E)$ holds true. For the Walsh process at hand, concrete choices for $A$ and $B$ are given by \begin{equation*} A^w=\begin{pmatrix} 0&0&0&\ldots&0&0\\ 1&-1&0&\ldots&0&0\\ 0&1&-1&\ldots&0&0\\ 0&0&1&\ldots &0&0\\ \vdots&\vdots&\vdots&\ddots&\vdots&\vdots\\ 0&0&0&\ldots&1&-1 \end{pmatrix},\ B^w=\begin{pmatrix} b_1&b_2&b_3&\ldots&b_{n-1}&b_n\\ 0&0&0&\ldots&0&0\\ 0&0&0&\ldots&0&0\\ \vdots&\vdots&\vdots&\ddots&\vdots&\vdots\\ 0&0&0&\ldots&0&0\\ 0&0&0&\ldots&0&0 \end{pmatrix}. \end{equation*} Then~\eqref{bc} is the condition that $f$ is actually continuous at the vertex $v$, i.e., $f(v_k)=f(v_m)$, $k$, $m=1,\dotsc,n$, and that~\eqref{eq2.2} is valid (with $w_k=b_k$, $k\in\ensuremath\{1,2,\dotsc,n\}$). Obviously, $(A^w, B^w)$ has maximal rank. However, $A^w (B^w)^\dagger$ is hermitian if and only if all $b_k$ are equal (i.e., $b_k = 1/n$, $\ensuremath k=1,\dotsc,n$). Nevertheless, \eqref{SE} exists also in the non-hermitian case, and $S_{A^w, B^w}(E)=S^w$ holds for all $E>0$ due to the relations $A^w S^w = - A^w$, and $B^w S^w = B^w$. In addition, the following relations are valid: \begin{align} \ensuremath S^w &= \bigl(\ensuremath S^w\bigr)^{-1}, \\ \det \ensuremath S^w &= (-1)^{n+1}. \end{align} Furthermore, $S^w$ is a contraction, and the associated Laplace operator is m-dissipative on $L^2(\mathcal{G})$ since trivially $\text{Im}(AB^\dagger)=0$, cf.\ Theorem~2.5 in~\cite{KoPo09c}. When all $b_k$ are equal, such that $A^w(B^w)^\dag=0$, then $S^w$ is an involutive, orthogonal matrix of the form \begin{equation} S^w = - 1 + 2P_n. \end{equation} $P_n$ is the matrix whose entries are equal to $1/n$. $P_n$ is a real orthogonal projection, that is $P_n = P_n^\dag = P_n^t = P_n^2$. It is also of rank $1$, that is $\dim \text{Ran} P_n = 1$. The relation~\eqref{eq2.4b} giving the resolvent in terms of the scattering matrix is actually valid in the more general context of arbitrary metric graphs and boundary conditions of the form~\eqref{bc}, see~\cite{KoSc06, KoPo09c}.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 3.2 via Dynkin's formula
nodes.statement: We proceed to show that the elastic Walsh process $\ensuremath W^e$ has a generator $A^e$ with domain $\mathcal{D}(A^e)$ which satisfies the boundary conditions as claimed. In other words, we claim that there exist $a\in(0,1)$ and $b_k\in (0,1)$, $k\in\ensuremath\{1,2,\dotsc,n\}$, with $a + \sum_k b_k =1$, so that for all $f\in\mathcal{D}(G)$, \begin{equation} a f(v) = \sum_{k=1}^n b_k f'(v_k) \end{equation} holds. To this end, we calculate $A^e f(v)$ in Dynkin's form. We shall use a notation similar to the one used in subsection~\ref{ssect1.5}. Namely, let $\ensuremath{\hat P}_v$ and $\ensuremath{\hat E}_v$ denote the probability and expectation, respectively, on the probability space extended by $(\mathbb{R}_+,\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}_+),P_\beta)$, while the corresponding symbols without $\hat{\,\cdot\,}$ are those for the Walsh process without killing. For $\epsilon>0$ and under $\ensuremath W^e$ let $\ensuremath H^e_{v,\epsilon}$ denote the hitting time of the complement $B_\epsilon(v)^c$ of the open ball $B_\epsilon(v)$ of radius $\epsilon>0$ with center $v$. Then $\ensuremath H^e_{v,\epsilon} = \ensuremath H^w_{v,\epsilon} \land \zeta_{\beta,0}$, where as before $\ensuremath H^w_{v,\epsilon}$ is the hitting time of $B_\epsilon(v)^c$ by the Walsh process $W$. (Note that $B_\epsilon(v)^c$ contains the cemetery $\Delta$.) We find \begin{equation} \ensuremath{\hat E}_v\Bigl(f\bigl(\ensuremath W^e(\ensuremath H^e_{v,\epsilon})\bigr)\Bigr) = \Bigl(\sum_{k=1}^n w_k f_k(\epsilon)\Bigr)\,\ensuremath{\hat P}_v\bigl(\ensuremath H^w_{v,\epsilon}<\zeta_{\beta,0}\bigr). \end{equation} The probability in the last expression is taken care of by the following lemma. \begin{lemma} For all $\epsilon$, $\beta>0$, \begin{equation} \ensuremath{\hat P}_v\bigl(\ensuremath H^w_{v,\epsilon} < \zeta_{\beta,0}\bigr) = \frac{1}{1+\epsilon\beta}. \end{equation} \end{lemma} \begin{proof} We may consider the Walsh process $W$ as being pathwise constructed from a standard Brownian motion $B$ on the real line as in the previous section, and we shall use the notations and conventions from there. Then it is clear that under $P_v$ and under $\ensuremath{\hat P}_v$, $\ensuremath H^w_{v,\epsilon}$ has the same law as the hitting time of the point $\epsilon$ in $\mathbb{R}_+$ by the reflecting Brownian motion $|B|$ under $Q_0$, that is, as $H^B_{\{-\epsilon,\epsilon\}}$ of the Brownian motion $B$ itself under $Q_0$. Let $K^w$ denote the right continuous pseudo-inverse of $L^w$. For fixed $s\in\mathbb{R}_+$ we get \begin{equation*} \{K^w_s < \ensuremath H^w_{v,\epsilon}\} = \{L^w(\ensuremath H^w_{v,\epsilon})>s\}. \end{equation*} Hence \begin{align*} P_v\bigl(K^w_s < \ensuremath H^w_{v,\epsilon}\bigr) &= P_v\bigl(L^w(\ensuremath H^w_{v,\epsilon})>s\bigr)\\ &= Q_0\bigl(L^B(H^B_{\{-\epsilon,\epsilon\}})>s\bigr). \end{align*} In appendix~B of~\cite{BMMG0} is shown with the method in~\cite[Section~6.4]{KaSh91} that under $Q_0$ the random variable $L^B(H^B_{\{-\epsilon,\epsilon\}})$ is exponentially distributed with mean $\epsilon$. So we find \begin{equation*} P_v\bigl(K^w_s < \ensuremath H^w_{v,\epsilon}\bigr) = e^{-s/\epsilon}. \end{equation*} We integrate this relation against the exponential law with rate $\beta$ in the variable $s$, and obtain \begin{align*} \ensuremath{\hat P}_v\bigl(\zeta_{\beta,0}>\ensuremath H^w_{v,\epsilon}\bigr) &= 1 - \beta\int_0^\infty e^{-\beta s}\,P_v\bigl(K^W_s < \ensuremath H^w_{v,\epsilon}\bigr)\,ds\\ &= \frac{1}{1+\epsilon\beta}. \end{align*} We used the fact that due to the continuity of the paths of $W$ we have $\zeta_{\beta,0}\ne \ensuremath H^w_{v,\epsilon}$. \end{proof} We insert formula~\eqref{eq3.2} into equation~\eqref{eq3.1a}, and obtain \begin{align*} A^e f(v) &= \lim_{\epsilon\ensuremath\downarrow 0}\, \frac{1}{\ensuremath{\hat E}_v(\ensuremath H^e_{v,\epsilon})} \,\Bigr(\ensuremath{\hat E}_v\Bigl(f\bigl(\ensuremath W^e(\ensuremath H^e_{v,\epsilon})\bigr)\Bigr) - f(v)\Bigl)\\ &= \lim_{\epsilon\ensuremath\downarrow 0}\, \frac{1}{\ensuremath{\hat E}_v(\ensuremath H^e_{v,\epsilon})} \,\Bigl(\frac{1}{1+\epsilon\beta}\,\sum_{k=1}^n w_k f_k(\epsilon) - f(v)\Bigr)\\ &= \lim_{\epsilon\ensuremath\downarrow 0}\, \frac{\epsilon}{\ensuremath{\hat E}_v(\ensuremath H^e_{v,\epsilon})} \frac{1}{1+\epsilon\beta}\,\Bigl(\sum_{k=1}^n w_k\,\frac{f_k(\epsilon)-f(v)}{\epsilon} -\beta f(v)\Bigr). \end{align*} Obviously $\ensuremath{\hat E}_v(\ensuremath H^e_{v,\epsilon})\le E_v(\ensuremath H^w_{v,\epsilon})=\epsilon^2$ (cf.~lemma~\ref{lem2.1}). Since the last limit and $f'(v_k)$, $k\in\ensuremath\{1,2,\dotsc,n\}$, exist and are finite, we get as a necessary condition \begin{equation} \sum_{k=1}^n w_k f'(v_k) - \beta f(v) =0. \end{equation} Thus we have proved the following theorem.

nodes.name: Second proof of Theorem 3.2 via the resolvent
nodes.statement: Next we compute the resolvent $\ensuremath R^e$ of the elastic Walsh process. As a byproduct this will give another proof of theorem~\ref{thm3.2}. Moreover, it will provide us with an explicit formula for the scattering matrix in this case. In contrast to the calculations in~\cite[Chapter~2.3]{ItMc74}, \cite[Chapter~6.2]{Kn81} for the classical case with $\mathcal{G}=\mathbb{R}_+$, we do not use the first passage time formula~\eqref{eq1.23}, but instead we use formula~\eqref{eq1.30}. This simplifies the computation considerably. Let $f\in\ensuremath C_0(\mathcal{G})$, $\lambda>0$, and $\xi\in\mathcal{G}$. In the present context formula~\eqref{eq1.30} reads \begin{equation*} R^e_\lambda f(\xi) = \ensuremath R^w_\lambda f(\xi) - e_\lambda(\xi)\,\ensuremath{\hat E}_v\bigl(e^{-\lambda \zeta_{\beta,0}}\bigr)\, \ensuremath R^w_\lambda f(v), \end{equation*} where $\ensuremath R^w$ is the resolvent of the Walsh process without killing, and $e_\lambda$ is defined in~\eqref{eq1.14}. The Laplace transform of the density of $\zeta_{\beta,0}$ under $\ensuremath{\hat P}_v$ is readily computed: \begin{lemma} For all $\lambda$, $\beta>0$, \begin{equation*} \ensuremath{\hat E}_v\bigl(e^{-\lambda \zeta_{\beta,0}}\bigr) = \frac{\beta}{\beta + \ensuremath\sqrt{2\lambda}}. \end{equation*} \end{lemma} \begin{proof} As remarked before, we may consider $L^w$ to be equal to the local time at the origin of the Brownian motion $B$ underlying the construction of $W$, and therefore the analogous statement is true for the right continuous pseudo-inverse $K^w$ of $L^w$. As above let $K^B$ denote the right continuous pseudo-inverse of $L^B$ (cf.~\ref{ssect1.2}). Then for $s\in\mathbb{R}_+$, \begin{align*} E_v\bigl(e^{-\lambda K^w_s}\bigr) &= E^Q_0\bigl(e^{-\lambda K^B_s}\bigr)\\ &= e^{-\ensuremath\sqrt{2\lambda} s}, \end{align*} where we used lemma~\ref{lem1.2}. Hence \begin{equation*} \ensuremath{\hat E}_v\bigl(e^{-\lambda \zeta_{\beta,0}}\bigr) = \beta \int_0^\infty e^{-(\beta+\ensuremath\sqrt{2\lambda}) t}\,dt, \end{equation*} which proves the lemma. \end{proof} With lemma~\ref{lem3.3} we obtain the following formula \begin{equation} R^e_\lambda f(\xi) = \ensuremath R^w_\lambda f(\xi) - \frac{\beta}{\beta + \ensuremath\sqrt{2\lambda}}\,e_\lambda(\xi)\, \ensuremath R^w_\lambda f(v). \end{equation} Note that $\ensuremath R^w_\lambda f$ is in the domain of the generator of the Walsh process, and therefore satisfies the boundary condition~\eqref{eq2.2}: \begin{equation*} \sum_{k=1}^n w_k\bigl(\ensuremath R^w_\lambda f\bigr)'(v_k) = 0. \end{equation*} On the other hand, we obviously have $e_\lambda'(v_k) = -\ensuremath\sqrt{2\lambda}$ for all $k\in\ensuremath\{1,2,\dotsc,n\}$. Thus with $\sum_{k=1}^n w_k =1$ we find, \begin{equation*} \sum_{k=1}^n w_k \bigl(R^e_\lambda f\bigr)'(v_k) = \beta\,\frac{\ensuremath\sqrt{2\lambda}}{\beta+\ensuremath\sqrt{2\lambda}}\,\ensuremath R^w_\lambda f(v), \end{equation*} while equation~\eqref{eq3.5} yields for $\xi=v$ \begin{equation*} R^e_\lambda f(v) = \frac{\ensuremath\sqrt{2\lambda}}{\beta+\ensuremath\sqrt{2\lambda}}\,\ensuremath R^w_\lambda f(v). \end{equation*} The last two equations show that for all $f\in\ensuremath C_0(\mathcal{G})$, $\lambda>0$, we have \begin{equation*} \sum_{k=1}^n w_k \bigl(R^e_\lambda f\bigr)'(v_k) = \beta\, R^e_\lambda f(v). \end{equation*} Since for every $\lambda>0$, $R^e_\lambda$ maps $\ensuremath C_0(\mathcal{G})$ onto the domain of the generator of $\ensuremath W^e$, we have another proof of theorem~\ref{thm3.2}.

nodes.statement: \ensuremath S^e_{km}(\lambda) = 2\,\frac{\ensuremath\sqrt{2\lambda}}{\beta+\ensuremath\sqrt{2\lambda}}\,w_m - \delta_{km},\qquad \lambda>0,\,k,m\in\ensuremath\{1,2,\dotsc,n\}.
nodes.section: 3 The Elastic Walsh Process
nodes.label: eq3.6c

nodes.name: Elastic scattering matrix and its data
nodes.statement: Note that in contrast to the case of the Walsh process, this time the scattering matrix is not constant with respect to $\lambda>0$. Also, when $\beta=0$, formula~\eqref{eq2.4c} is recovered, as it should be. In analogy with the discussion in remark~\ref{rem2.4}, the boundary conditions for the elastic Walsh process is given by the matrices \begin{equation*} A^e = \begin{pmatrix} 0&0&0&\ldots&0&\beta\\ 1&-1&0&\ldots&0&0\\ 0&1&-1&\ldots&0&0\\ 0&0&1&\ldots &0&0\\ \vdots&\vdots&\vdots&\ddots&\vdots&\vdots\\ 0&0&0&\ldots&1&-1 \end{pmatrix},\ B^e=\begin{pmatrix} w_1&w_2&w_3&\ldots&w_{n-1}&w_n\\ 0&0&0&\ldots&0&0\\ 0&0&0&\ldots&0&0\\ 0&0&0&\ldots&0&0\\ \vdots&\vdots&\vdots&\ddots&\vdots&\vdots\\ 0&0&0&\ldots&0&0 \end{pmatrix}, \end{equation*} such that \begin{align*} \ensuremath S^e(\lambda) &= S_{A^e,B^e}(E=-2\lambda)\\ &= - (A^e+\ensuremath\sqrt{2\lambda} B^e)^{-1}\,(A^e-\ensuremath\sqrt{2\lambda} B^e). \end{align*} Observe that for $k$, $m\in\{1,\dotsc,n\}$ the matrix element $\ensuremath S^e_{km}(\lambda)$ of the scattering matrix is obtained from the resolvent kernel as \begin{equation*} \ensuremath S^e_{km}(\lambda) = \ensuremath\sqrt{2\lambda}\,\lim_{\xi,\,\eta\to v}\bigl(\ensuremath r^e_\lambda(\xi,\eta) - r_\lambda(\xi,\eta)\bigr), \end{equation*} where the limit on the right hand side is taken in such a way that $\xi$, $\eta$ converge to $v$ along the edges $l_k$, $l_m$ respectively. $\ensuremath S^e_{km}(\lambda)$ in turn fixes the data $w_m$ and $\beta$, e.g., via the behavior for large $\lambda$, that is from the behavior at ``large energies'' \begin{equation*} w_m = \frac{1}{2}\bigl(\delta_{km} + \lim_{\lambda'\ensuremath\uparrow\infty} \ensuremath S^e_{km}(\lambda')\bigr), \quad \text{for all $k\in\ensuremath\{1,2,\dotsc,n\}$}, \end{equation*} and \begin{equation*} \beta = \ensuremath\sqrt{2\lambda}\Bigl(\frac{\delta_{km}+\lim_{\lambda'\ensuremath\uparrow\infty}\ensuremath S^e_{km}(\lambda')} {\delta_{km}+\ensuremath S^e_{mm}(\lambda)}-1\Bigr),\quad \text{for all $\lambda$, and all $k$, $m\in\ensuremath\{1,2,\dotsc,n\}$}. \end{equation*} Alternatively, the data can be obtained from the small $\lambda$ behavior, that is the threshold behavior, of the scattering matrix, since from \begin{equation*} \frac{w_m}{\beta} = \lim_{\lambda \ensuremath\downarrow 0} \frac{1}{2\ensuremath\sqrt{2\lambda}}\bigl(\ensuremath S^e_{km}(\lambda)+\delta_{km}\bigr) \qquad \text{for all $k\in\ensuremath\{1,2,\dotsc,n\}$}, \end{equation*} we obtain \begin{equation*} \beta^{-1} = \frac{1}{2\ensuremath\sqrt{2\lambda}}\Bigl(\sum_{m=1}^n\ensuremath S^e_{km}(\lambda)+1\Bigr) \qquad \text{for all $k\in\ensuremath\{1,2,\dotsc,n\}$}, \end{equation*} and therefore \begin{equation*} w_m = \frac{\lim_{\lambda\ensuremath\downarrow 0} \lambda^{-1/2}\bigl(\ensuremath S^e_{km}(\lambda)+\delta_{km}\bigr)} {\lim_{\lambda\ensuremath\downarrow 0} \lambda^{-1/2}\Bigl(\sum_m\ensuremath S^e_{k'm}(\lambda)+1\Bigr)} \qquad \text{for all $k$, $k'\in\ensuremath\{1,2,\dotsc,n\}$}. \end{equation*} Furthermore we remark that in the context of quantum mechanics in the self-adjoint case $w_k=1/n$, $\ensuremath k=1,\dotsc,n$, the boundary conditions of the elastic Walsh process are interpreted as the presence of a $\delta$--potential of strength $\beta$ at the vertex.
nodes.section: 3 The Elastic Walsh Process
nodes.statement_short: The elastic scattering matrix is energy dependent, comes from boundary matrices $A^e,B^e$, and its high and low energy limits recover $w_m$ and $\beta$.
nodes.label: rem3.5

nodes.name: Inverse Laplace transform (3.7)
nodes.statement: \frac{\ensuremath\sqrt{2\lambda}}{\beta+\ensuremath\sqrt{2\lambda}}\quad &\mathop{\longrightarrow}^{\mathcal{L}^{-1}}\quad \epsilon_0(dt) - \beta\Bigl(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi t}}-\frac{\beta}{2}e^{\beta^2 t/2} \mathop{\operator@font erfc}\nolimits\Bigl(\beta\sqrt{\frac{t}{2}}\Bigr)\Bigr)\,dt,
nodes.section: 3 The Elastic Walsh Process
nodes.label: eq3.7

nodes.name: Inverse Laplace transform (3.8)
nodes.statement: \frac{1}{\beta+\ensuremath\sqrt{2\lambda}}\,e^{-\ensuremath\sqrt{2\lambda} x}\quad &\mathop{\longrightarrow}^{\mathcal{L}^{-1}}\quad g(t,x) - \frac{\beta}{2}\,e^{\beta x+ \beta^2 t/2} \mathop{\operator@font erfc}\nolimits\Bigl(\frac{x}{\sqrt{2t}}+\beta\sqrt{\frac{t}{2}}\Bigr).
nodes.section: 3 The Elastic Walsh Process
nodes.label: eq3.8

nodes.name: Inverse Laplace transform of the elastic scattering matrix
nodes.statement: Then the inverse Laplace transform of the scattering matrix $\ensuremath S^e$ is given by the following measures on $\mathbb{R}_+$: \begin{equation} \begin{split} \ensuremath s^e_{km}(dt) = (2w_m-\delta_{km})\,\epsilon_0(dt) &- 2w_m\beta\,\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi t}}\,dt\\ & + w_m\beta^2 e^{\beta^2t/2}\,\mathop{\operator@font erfc}\nolimits\Bigl(\beta\sqrt{\frac{t}{2}}\Bigr)\,dt, \end{split} \end{equation} with $k$, $m\in\ensuremath\{1,2,\dotsc,n\}$.
nodes.section: 3 The Elastic Walsh Process

nodes.name: Inverse Laplace transform of the elastic scattering matrix
nodes.statement: \begin{split} \ensuremath s^e_{km}(dt) = (2w_m-\delta_{km})\,\epsilon_0(dt) &- 2w_m\beta\,\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi t}}\,dt\\ & + w_m\beta^2 e^{\beta^2t/2}\,\mathop{\operator@font erfc}\nolimits\Bigl(\beta\sqrt{\frac{t}{2}}\Bigr)\,dt, \end{split}
nodes.section: 3 The Elastic Walsh Process
nodes.label: eq3.9

nodes.name: Kernel g_{beta,0}
nodes.statement: Moreover, for $t>0$, $x\ge 0$, let us introduce \begin{equation} g_{\beta,0}(t,x) = g(t,x) - \frac{\beta}{2}\,e^{\beta x+ \beta^2 t/2} \mathop{\operator@font erfc}\nolimits\Bigl(\frac{x}{\sqrt{2t}}+\beta\sqrt{\frac{t}{2}}\Bigr). \end{equation}
nodes.section: 3 The Elastic Walsh Process

nodes.name: Kernel g_{beta,0}
nodes.statement: g_{\beta,0}(t,x) = g(t,x) - \frac{\beta}{2}\,e^{\beta x+ \beta^2 t/2} \mathop{\operator@font erfc}\nolimits\Bigl(\frac{x}{\sqrt{2t}}+\beta\sqrt{\frac{t}{2}}\Bigr).
nodes.section: 3 The Elastic Walsh Process
nodes.label: eq3.10

nodes.name: Transition density of the elastic Walsh process
nodes.statement: For $t>0$, $\xi$, $\eta\in\mathcal{G}$, the transition density $\ensuremath p^e$ of the elastic Walsh process is given by \begin{equation} \ensuremath p^e(t,\xi,\eta) = p^D(t,\xi,\eta) + \sum_{k,m=1}^n \onel(\xi)\, 2w_m\,g_{\beta,0}\bigl(t,d_v(\xi,\eta)\bigr)\, \onel[m](\eta), \end{equation} and alternatively by \begin{equation} \begin{split} \ensuremath p^e(t,\xi,\eta) = p(t,\xi,\eta) + \sum_{k,m=1}^n &\onel(\xi)\,\Bigl(\int_0^t P_\xi(\ensuremath H^w_v\in ds)\\ &\times \Bigl(\ensuremath s^e_{km}*g\bigl(\cdot,d(v,\eta)\bigr)\Bigr)(t-s)\, \Bigr)\,\onel[m](\eta), \end{split} \end{equation} where $*$ denotes convolution.
nodes.section: 3 The Elastic Walsh Process
nodes.label: lem3.6

nodes.name: Elastic Walsh transition density
nodes.statement: \ensuremath p^e(t,\xi,\eta) = p^D(t,\xi,\eta) + \sum_{k,m=1}^n \onel(\xi)\, 2w_m\,g_{\beta,0}\bigl(t,d_v(\xi,\eta)\bigr)\, \onel[m](\eta),
nodes.section: 3 The Elastic Walsh Process
nodes.label: eq3.11

nodes.name: Elastic Walsh transition density via the hitting time
nodes.statement: \begin{split} \ensuremath p^e(t,\xi,\eta) = p(t,\xi,\eta) + \sum_{k,m=1}^n &\onel(\xi)\,\Bigl(\int_0^t P_\xi(\ensuremath H^w_v\in ds)\\ &\times \Bigl(\ensuremath s^e_{km}*g\bigl(\cdot,d(v,\eta)\bigr)\Bigr)(t-s)\, \Bigr)\,\onel[m](\eta), \end{split}
nodes.section: 3 The Elastic Walsh Process
nodes.label: eq3.12

nodes.name: Filtration F^w of the Walsh process
nodes.statement: Consider the Walsh process $W$ on $\mathcal{G}$ from section~\ref{sect2} together with a right continuous, complete filtration $\ensuremath \mathcal{F}^w$, relative to which it is strongly Markovian.
nodes.section: 4 The Walsh Process with a Sticky Vertex

nodes.name: Time change tau
nodes.statement: For $\gamma\ge 0$ introduce a new time scale $\tau$ by \begin{equation} \tau^{-1}: t\mapsto t + \gamma L^w_t, \qquad t\ge 0. \end{equation}
nodes.section: 4 The Walsh Process with a Sticky Vertex

nodes.name: Time change tau
nodes.statement: \tau^{-1}: t\mapsto t + \gamma L^w_t, \qquad t\ge 0.
nodes.section: 4 The Walsh Process with a Sticky Vertex
nodes.label: eq4.1

nodes.name: tau is a strictly increasing bijection
nodes.statement: Since $L^w$ is non-decreasing, $\tau^{-1}$ is strictly increasing. Moreover, we have $\tau^{-1}(0)=0$ and $\lim_{t\to+\infty}\tau^{-1}(t) = +\infty$, which implies that $\tau$ exists, and is strictly increasing from $\mathbb{R}+$ onto $\mathbb{R}_+$, too.
nodes.section: 4 The Walsh Process with a Sticky Vertex
conclusions: $\tau$ exists, and is strictly increasing from $\mathbb{R}+$ onto $\mathbb{R}_+$, too

nodes.name: Additivity of the time change
nodes.statement: For all $s$, $t\ge 0$, a.s.\ the following formula holds true \begin{equation} \tau(s+t) = \tau(s) + \tau(t)\circ \theta_{\tau(s)}. \end{equation}
nodes.section: 4 The Walsh Process with a Sticky Vertex
nodes.label: lem4.1

nodes.name: Additivity of tau
nodes.statement: \tau(s+t) = \tau(s) + \tau(t)\circ \theta_{\tau(s)}.
nodes.section: 4 The Walsh Process with a Sticky Vertex
nodes.label: eq4.2

nodes.name: Time-changed filtration F^s
nodes.statement: It is easily checked that for every $t\ge 0$, $\tau(t)$ is an $\ensuremath \mathcal{F}^w$--stopping time, and since $\tau$ is increasing, we obtain the subfiltration $\ensuremath \mathcal{F}^s = (\ensuremath \mathcal{F}^s_t,\,t\ge 0)$ of $\ensuremath \mathcal{F}^w$ defined by $\ensuremath \mathcal{F}^s_t = \ensuremath \mathcal{F}^w_{\tau(t)}$, $t\in\mathbb{R}_+$.
nodes.section: 4 The Walsh Process with a Sticky Vertex

nodes.name: F^s is complete and right continuous
nodes.statement: Standard calculations show that the completeness and the right continuity of $\ensuremath \mathcal{F}^w$ entail the same properties for $\mathcal{F}^s$. (For details of the argument in the case where $\mathcal{G}=\mathbb{R}_+$ we refer the interested reader to section~3 of~\cite{BMMG0}.)
nodes.section: 4 The Walsh Process with a Sticky Vertex
conclusions: the completeness and the right continuity of $\ensuremath \mathcal{F}^w$ entail the same properties for $\mathcal{F}^s$

nodes.name: Walsh process with sticky vertex
nodes.statement: Define a stochastic process $\ensuremath W^s$ on $\mathcal{G}$, called \emph{Walsh process with sticky vertex}, by \begin{equation} \ensuremath W^s_t = W_{\tau(t)},\qquad t\in\mathbb{R}_+. \end{equation}
nodes.section: 4 The Walsh Process with a Sticky Vertex

nodes.name: Walsh process with sticky vertex
nodes.statement: \ensuremath W^s_t = W_{\tau(t)},\qquad t\in\mathbb{R}_+.
nodes.section: 4 The Walsh Process with a Sticky Vertex
nodes.label: eq4.3

nodes.name: Heuristics of stickiness
nodes.statement: Observe that when $W$ is away from the vertex, $L^w$ is constant, and therefore in this case $\tau^{-1}$ grows with rate $1$. On the other hand, when $W$ is at the vertex, $\tau^{-1}$ grows faster than with rate $1$, and therefore $\tau$ increases slower than the deterministic time scale $t\mapsto t$. Thus $\ensuremath W^s$ ``experiences a slow down in time'' until $W$ has left the vertex. In this heuristic sense the vertex is ``sticky'' for $\ensuremath W^s$, because it spends more time there than $W$.
nodes.section: 4 The Walsh Process with a Sticky Vertex

nodes.name: W^s is continuous and adapted
nodes.statement: Note that because $L^w$ has continuous paths, $\tau^{-1}$ and therefore also $\tau$ are pathwise continuous. Consequently, $\ensuremath W^s$ has continuous sample paths. Since $W$ has continuous paths, it is a measurable process, and hence for every $t\ge 0$, $W_{\tau(t)}$ is $\ensuremath \mathcal{F}^w_{\tau(t)}$--measurable, that is, $\ensuremath W^s$ is $\ensuremath \mathcal{F}^s$--adapted.
nodes.section: 4 The Walsh Process with a Sticky Vertex

nodes.name: Shift operators theta^s
nodes.statement: Set $\theta^s_t = \theta_{\tau(t)}$.
nodes.section: 4 The Walsh Process with a Sticky Vertex

nodes.name: theta^s are shift operators for W^s
nodes.statement: With the additivity~\eqref{eq4.2} of $\tau$ we immediately find \begin{equation} W^s_s\circ\theta^s_t = W^s_{s+t},\qquad s,\,t\in\mathbb{R}_+. \end{equation} Thus $\theta^s=(\theta^s_t,\,t\in\mathbb{R}_+)$ is a family of shift operators for $\ensuremath W^s$.
nodes.section: 4 The Walsh Process with a Sticky Vertex

nodes.name: Shift operators for W^s
nodes.statement: W^s_s\circ\theta^s_t = W^s_{s+t},\qquad s,\,t\in\mathbb{R}_+.
nodes.section: 4 The Walsh Process with a Sticky Vertex
nodes.label: sshift

nodes.name: Proof that W^s is a Brownian motion on G
nodes.statement: Next we show the strong Markov property of $\ensuremath W^s$ relative to $\ensuremath \mathcal{F}^s$ following the argument briefly sketched in section~6.2 of~\cite{Kn81} for the case $\mathcal{G}=\mathbb{R}_+$. First we prove the simple Markov property of $\ensuremath W^s$ with respect to $\ensuremath \mathcal{F}^s$. To this end, let $s$, $t\ge 0$, $\xi\in\mathcal{G}$, and $C\in\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{G})$. Then we get with~\eqref{sshift} \begin{align*} P_\xi\bigl(\ensuremath W^s_{t+s}\in C\ensuremath\,\big|\, \ensuremath \mathcal{F}^s_t\bigr) &= P_\xi\bigl(\ensuremath W^s_s\circ\theta^s_t\in C\ensuremath\,\big|\, \ensuremath \mathcal{F}^s_t\bigr)\\ &= P_\xi\bigl(W_{\tau(s)}\circ\theta_{\tau(t)}\in C\ensuremath\,\big|\, \ensuremath \mathcal{F}^w_{\tau(t)}\bigr)\\ &= P_{W_{\tau(t)}} \bigl(W_{\tau(s)}\in C\bigr)\\ &= P_{\ensuremath W^s_t}\bigl(\ensuremath W^s_s\in C\bigr), \end{align*} where we used the strong Markov property of $W$ with respect to $\ensuremath \mathcal{F}^w$. As a next step we prove that $\ensuremath W^s$ has the strong Markov property for its hitting time $H^s_v$ of the vertex. By construction, $\ensuremath W^s$ and $W$ have the same paths up to the hitting time of the vertex, and in particular $H^s_v$ is also the hitting time of the vertex by $W$, that is, $H^s_v=H_v$. Moreover, since $L^w(H_v)=0$, we get that $\tau^{-1}(H_v) = H_v = \tau(H_v)$, as well as $\theta^s(H_v) = \theta(H_v)$. Assume now that $t\ge 0$, $\xi\in\mathcal{G}$, and $C\in\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{G})$. Then on $\{H_v<+\infty\}$ we can compute with the strong Markov property of $W$ as follows \begin{align*} P_\xi\bigl(\ensuremath W^s_{t+H_v}\in C \ensuremath\,\big|\, \ensuremath \mathcal{F}^w_{H_v}\bigr) &= P_\xi\bigl(\ensuremath W^s_t\circ\theta^s_{H_v}\in C\ensuremath\,\big|\, \ensuremath \mathcal{F}^w_{H_v}\bigr)\\ &= P_\xi\bigl(W_{\tau(t)}\circ\theta_{H_v}\in C\ensuremath\,\big|\, \ensuremath \mathcal{F}^w_{H_v}\bigr)\\ &= P_v\bigl(W_{\tau(t)}\in C\bigr)\\ &= P_v\bigl(\ensuremath W^s_t\in C\bigr). \end{align*} It is readily checked that $\ensuremath \mathcal{F}^s_{H_v}\subset\ensuremath \mathcal{F}^w_{H_v}$, and therefore we get in particular the strong Markov property of $W^s$ with respect to $H^s_v=H_v$ in the form \begin{equation} P_\xi\bigl(\ensuremath W^s_{t+H^s_v}\in C \ensuremath\,\big|\, \ensuremath \mathcal{F}^s_{H_v}\bigr) = P_v\bigl(\ensuremath W^s_t\in C\bigr). \end{equation} Finally, with the strong Markov property of the standard one-dimensional Brownian motions on every edge and the strong Markov property~\eqref{sSMT_v} just proved we can apply the arguments similar to those in~\cite[Section 3.6]{ItMc74} to conclude that $W^s$ is a Feller process. Hence it is strongly Markovian relative to the filtration $\mathcal{F}^s$. By construction, $W^s$ is up to time $H^s_v$ equivalent to a standard one-dimensional Brownian motion, and it has continuous sample paths.
nodes.section: 4 The Walsh Process with a Sticky Vertex
nodes.statement_short: Simple Markov property from the time change and the strong Markov property of $W$, strong Markov at $H_v$, then Feller arguments. The key step is $\tau(H_v)=H_v$, so $W^s$ restarts at $v$ like $W$.

nodes.name: Plan
nodes.statement: Next we show the strong Markov property of $\ensuremath W^s$ relative to $\ensuremath \mathcal{F}^s$ following the argument briefly sketched in section~6.2 of~\cite{Kn81} for the case $\mathcal{G}=\mathbb{R}_+$.
nodes.section: 4 The Walsh Process with a Sticky Vertex
nodes.statement_short: Plan following Knight's sketch.

nodes.name: Simple Markov property
nodes.statement: First we prove the simple Markov property of $\ensuremath W^s$ with respect to $\ensuremath \mathcal{F}^s$. To this end, let $s$, $t\ge 0$, $\xi\in\mathcal{G}$, and $C\in\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{G})$. Then we get with~\eqref{sshift} \begin{align*} P_\xi\bigl(\ensuremath W^s_{t+s}\in C\ensuremath\,\big|\, \ensuremath \mathcal{F}^s_t\bigr) &= P_\xi\bigl(\ensuremath W^s_s\circ\theta^s_t\in C\ensuremath\,\big|\, \ensuremath \mathcal{F}^s_t\bigr)\\ &= P_\xi\bigl(W_{\tau(s)}\circ\theta_{\tau(t)}\in C\ensuremath\,\big|\, \ensuremath \mathcal{F}^w_{\tau(t)}\bigr)\\ &= P_{W_{\tau(t)}} \bigl(W_{\tau(s)}\in C\bigr)\\ &= P_{\ensuremath W^s_t}\bigl(\ensuremath W^s_s\in C\bigr), \end{align*} where we used the strong Markov property of $W$ with respect to $\ensuremath \mathcal{F}^w$.
nodes.section: 4 The Walsh Process with a Sticky Vertex
nodes.statement_short: Simple Markov property via the shift identity and the strong Markov property of $W$.

nodes.name: Same hitting time
nodes.statement: As a next step we prove that $\ensuremath W^s$ has the strong Markov property for its hitting time $H^s_v$ of the vertex. By construction, $\ensuremath W^s$ and $W$ have the same paths up to the hitting time of the vertex, and in particular $H^s_v$ is also the hitting time of the vertex by $W$, that is, $H^s_v=H_v$. Moreover, since $L^w(H_v)=0$, we get that $\tau^{-1}(H_v) = H_v = \tau(H_v)$, as well as $\theta^s(H_v) = \theta(H_v)$.
nodes.section: 4 The Walsh Process with a Sticky Vertex
nodes.statement_short: Hitting times of the vertex and shifts coincide for $W^s$ and $W$.

nodes.name: Strong Markov at H_v
nodes.statement: Assume now that $t\ge 0$, $\xi\in\mathcal{G}$, and $C\in\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{G})$. Then on $\{H_v<+\infty\}$ we can compute with the strong Markov property of $W$ as follows \begin{align*} P_\xi\bigl(\ensuremath W^s_{t+H_v}\in C \ensuremath\,\big|\, \ensuremath \mathcal{F}^w_{H_v}\bigr) &= P_\xi\bigl(\ensuremath W^s_t\circ\theta^s_{H_v}\in C\ensuremath\,\big|\, \ensuremath \mathcal{F}^w_{H_v}\bigr)\\ &= P_\xi\bigl(W_{\tau(t)}\circ\theta_{H_v}\in C\ensuremath\,\big|\, \ensuremath \mathcal{F}^w_{H_v}\bigr)\\ &= P_v\bigl(W_{\tau(t)}\in C\bigr)\\ &= P_v\bigl(\ensuremath W^s_t\in C\bigr). \end{align*}
nodes.section: 4 The Walsh Process with a Sticky Vertex
nodes.statement_short: Strong Markov property of $W$ at $H_v$.

nodes.name: Filtration
nodes.statement: It is readily checked that $\ensuremath \mathcal{F}^s_{H_v}\subset\ensuremath \mathcal{F}^w_{H_v}$, and therefore we get in particular the strong Markov property of $W^s$ with respect to $H^s_v=H_v$ in the form \begin{equation} P_\xi\bigl(\ensuremath W^s_{t+H^s_v}\in C \ensuremath\,\big|\, \ensuremath \mathcal{F}^s_{H_v}\bigr) = P_v\bigl(\ensuremath W^s_t\in C\bigr). \end{equation}
nodes.section: 4 The Walsh Process with a Sticky Vertex
nodes.statement_short: Pass to the smaller filtration to get the strong Markov property at $H_v$.

nodes.name: Strong Markov property of W^s at H_v
nodes.statement: P_\xi\bigl(\ensuremath W^s_{t+H^s_v}\in C \ensuremath\,\big|\, \ensuremath \mathcal{F}^s_{H_v}\bigr) = P_v\bigl(\ensuremath W^s_t\in C\bigr).
nodes.section: 4 The Walsh Process with a Sticky Vertex
nodes.label: sSMT_v

nodes.name: Feller property
nodes.statement: Finally, with the strong Markov property of the standard one-dimensional Brownian motions on every edge and the strong Markov property~\eqref{sSMT_v} just proved we can apply the arguments similar to those in~\cite[Section 3.6]{ItMc74} to conclude that $W^s$ is a Feller process. Hence it is strongly Markovian relative to the filtration $\mathcal{F}^s$.
nodes.section: 4 The Walsh Process with a Sticky Vertex
nodes.statement_short: Feller arguments of Ito-McKean give the strong Markov property.

nodes.name: Path properties
nodes.statement: By construction, $W^s$ is up to time $H^s_v$ equivalent to a standard one-dimensional Brownian motion, and it has continuous sample paths.
nodes.section: 4 The Walsh Process with a Sticky Vertex
nodes.statement_short: Before $H_v$ it is an edge Brownian motion with continuous paths.

nodes.name: W^s is a Brownian motion on G
nodes.statement: Hence, altogether we have shown that $\ensuremath W^s$ is a Brownian motion on $\mathcal{G}$ in the sense of definition~\ref{def_BM}.
nodes.section: 4 The Walsh Process with a Sticky Vertex
conclusions: $\ensuremath W^s$ is a Brownian motion on $\mathcal{G}$ in the sense of definition~\ref{def_BM}

nodes.name: The vertex is not a trap for W^s
nodes.statement: Now we want to compute the generator of $\ensuremath W^s$, and first we argue that $v$ is not a trap for $\ensuremath W^s$.
nodes.section: 4 The Walsh Process with a Sticky Vertex
conclusions: $v$ is not a trap for $\ensuremath W^s$

nodes.name: Proof that the vertex is not a trap
nodes.statement: To this end, we may consider $W$ as constructed from a standard Brownian motion $B$ as described in section~\ref{sect2}. Let $Z$ denote the zero set of $B$. Given $s\ge 0$ we can choose $t_0\ge s$ in the complement $Z^c$ of $Z$. Consider $t = \tau^{-1}(t_0)$, i.e., $t = t_0 + \gamma L^w_{t_0}$. Obviously $t\ge s$, and $\tau(t)\in Z^c$. Therefore $B_{\tau(t)} \ne 0$, and consequently $\ensuremath W^s_t=W_{\tau(t)}\ne v$.
nodes.section: 4 The Walsh Process with a Sticky Vertex
nodes.statement_short: For any $s$ pick $t_0\ge s$ off the zero set of $B$; then $t=\tau^{-1}(t_0)\ge s$ and $W^s_t\ne v$.

nodes.name: Pathwise construction
nodes.statement: To this end, we may consider $W$ as constructed from a standard Brownian motion $B$ as described in section~\ref{sect2}.
nodes.section: 4 The Walsh Process with a Sticky Vertex
nodes.statement_short: Use the pathwise construction from $B$.

nodes.name: Choose t_0
nodes.statement: Let $Z$ denote the zero set of $B$. Given $s\ge 0$ we can choose $t_0\ge s$ in the complement $Z^c$ of $Z$.
nodes.section: 4 The Walsh Process with a Sticky Vertex
nodes.statement_short: Choose $t_0\ge s$ off the zero set.

nodes.name: Set t
nodes.statement: Consider $t = \tau^{-1}(t_0)$, i.e., $t = t_0 + \gamma L^w_{t_0}$. Obviously $t\ge s$, and $\tau(t)\in Z^c$.
nodes.section: 4 The Walsh Process with a Sticky Vertex

nodes.name: Conclusion
nodes.statement: Therefore $B_{\tau(t)} \ne 0$, and consequently $\ensuremath W^s_t=W_{\tau(t)}\ne v$.
nodes.section: 4 The Walsh Process with a Sticky Vertex
nodes.statement_short: Hence $W^s_t\ne v$.

nodes.name: Generator of the sticky Walsh process
nodes.statement: Consider the boundary condition~\eqref{eq1.1} with $a=0$, $c\in(0,1)$, and $b\in [0,1]^n$. Set \begin{equation} w_k = \frac{b_k}{1-c},\,\ensuremath k=1,\dotsc,n,\qquad \gamma = \frac{c}{1-c}, \end{equation} and let $\ensuremath W^s$ be the sticky Walsh process as constructed above with these parameters. Then the generator $A^s$ of $\ensuremath W^s$ is $1/2$ times the second derivative on $\mathcal{G}$ with domain consisting of those $f\in\ensuremath C_0^2(\mathcal{G})$ which satisfy condition~\eqref{eq1.1b}.
nodes.section: 4 The Walsh Process with a Sticky Vertex
assumptions: Consider the boundary condition~\eqref{eq1.1} with $a=0$, $c\in(0,1)$, and $b\in [0,1]^n$.
let $\ensuremath W^s$ be the sticky Walsh process as constructed above with these parameters
conclusions: the generator $A^s$ of $\ensuremath W^s$ is $1/2$ times the second derivative on $\mathcal{G}$ with domain consisting of those $f\in\ensuremath C_0^2(\mathcal{G})$ which satisfy condition~\eqref{eq1.1b}
nodes.statement_short: The sticky Walsh process with $w_k=b_k/(1-c)$, $\gamma=c/(1-c)$ realizes the boundary condition with $a=0$.
nodes.label: thm4.2

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4.3
nodes.statement: Let $W$, and therefore also $\ensuremath W^s$, start in the vertex $v$. Since $\ensuremath W^s$ and $W$ have continuous paths with infinite lifetime we have for all $\gamma\ge 0$ \begin{equation*} \ensuremath H^s_{v,\epsilon} = \inf\bigl\{t>0,\, d(v,W_{\tau(t)})=\epsilon\bigr\}, \end{equation*} and in particular for $\gamma=0$, \begin{equation*} \ensuremath H^w_{v,\epsilon} = \inf\bigl\{t>0,\, d(v,W_t)=\epsilon\bigr\}. \end{equation*} Moreover, as argued above, both infima are a.s.\ finite. Set \begin{equation*} \sigma = \ensuremath H^w_{v,\epsilon} + \gamma\,L^w_{\ensuremath H^w_{v,\epsilon}}. \end{equation*} Then $\tau(\sigma) = \ensuremath H^w_{v,\epsilon}$, and therefore \begin{align*} d\bigl(v, \ensuremath W^s_\sigma\bigr) &= d\bigl(v, W_{\tau(\sigma)}\bigr)\\ &= d\bigl(v, W_{\ensuremath H^w_{v,\epsilon}}\bigr)\\ &= \epsilon. \end{align*} Consequently we get $\ensuremath H^s_{v,\epsilon} \le \sigma$. To derive the converse inequality we remark that \begin{align*} \epsilon &= d\bigl(v, \ensuremath W^s_{\ensuremath H^s_{v,\epsilon}}\bigr)\\ &= d\bigl(v, W_{\tau(\ensuremath H^s_{v,\epsilon})}\bigr), \end{align*} which implies \begin{equation*} \tau\bigl(\ensuremath H^s_{v,\epsilon}\bigr)\ge \ensuremath H^w_{v,\epsilon}. \end{equation*} Since $\tau$ is strictly increasing this entails \begin{equation*} \ensuremath H^s_{v,\epsilon} \ge \tau^{-1}\bigl(\ensuremath H^w_{v,\epsilon}\bigr) = \sigma, \end{equation*} and the proof is finished.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 4.2
nodes.statement: Let $w_k$, $\ensuremath k=1,\dotsc,n$, and $\gamma$ be defined as in~\eqref{eq4.4}, and note that due to the condition~\eqref{eq1.1a} on $b_k$, $\ensuremath k=1,\dotsc,n$, and $c$, we have $w_k\in [0,1]$, $\ensuremath k=1,\dotsc,n$, $\sum_k w_k =1$, as well as $\gamma>0$. Then we have for $f\in\mathcal{D}(A^s)$, $A^s f(v) = 1/2 f''(v)$ (cf.\ theorem~\ref{thm_Feller}). nodes.name: Second proof of Theorem 4.2 via the resolvent
nodes.statement: Next we shall compute the resolvent $\ensuremath R^s$ of the Walsh process with sticky vertex. Similarly to the alternative proof of theorem~\ref{thm3.2} for the elastic Walsh process, as a byproduct we obtain an alternative proof of theorem~\ref{thm4.2}. We begin with the following \begin{lemma} Let $\lambda>0$, $f\in \ensuremath C_0(\mathcal{G})$. Then \begin{equation} \frac{1}{2} \bigl(\ensuremath R^s_\lambda f\bigr)''(v) = \frac{1}{\ensuremath\sqrt{2\lambda} +\gamma\lambda}\,\Bigl(2\lambda\,(e^w_\lambda,f) - \ensuremath\sqrt{2\lambda} f(v)\Bigr) \end{equation} holds, where \begin{equation} e^w_\lambda(\xi) = w_k\,e_\lambda(\xi),\qquad \xi\in l_k,\,\ensuremath k=1,\dotsc,n, \end{equation} and $e_\lambda$ is defined in equation~\eqref{eq1.14}. \end{lemma} \begin{proof} Let $A^s$ be the generator of $\ensuremath W^s$ on $\ensuremath C_0(\mathcal{G})$. From the identity $A^s \ensuremath R^s_\lambda = \lambda\,\ensuremath R^s_\lambda -\text{id}$, and the definition of $\tau$ we get \begin{align*} \frac{1}{2}\,\bigl(\ensuremath R^s_\lambda f\bigr)''(v) &= \lambda E_v\Bigl(\int_0^\infty e^{-\lambda t}\bigl(f(\ensuremath W^s_t)-f(v)\bigr)\,dt\Bigr)\\ &= \lambda E_v\Bigl(\int_0^\infty e^{-\lambda(s+\gamma L^w_s)} \bigl(f(W_s)-f(v)\bigr)\,(ds + \gamma dL^w_s)\Bigr)\\ &= \lambda E_v\Bigl(\int_0^\infty e^{-\lambda(s+\gamma L^w_s)} \bigl(f(W_s)-f(v)\bigr)\,ds \Bigr). \end{align*} In the last equality we used the fact that $L^w$ only grows when $W$ is at the vertex~$v$. By construction of the Walsh process $W$ we have \begin{align*} E_v\Bigl(&e^{-\lambda\gamma L^w_s}\bigl(f(W_s)-f(v)\bigr)\Bigr)\\ &= \sum_{k=1}^n w_k\,E_0\Bigl(e^{-\lambda\gamma L^B_s} \bigl(f_k(|B_s|) - f_k(0)\bigr) \Bigr)\\ &= 2\sum_{k=1}^n w_k \int_0^\infty \int_0^\infty e^{-\lambda\gamma y} \bigl(f_k(x) - f_k(0)\bigr)\,\frac{x+y}{\sqrt{2\pi s^3}}\, e^{-(x+y)^2/2s}\,dx\,dy, \end{align*} where we used lemma~\ref{lem1.1}. We insert the last expression above, and use formula~\eqref{LT}. This gives \begin{align*} \frac{1}{2}\,\bigl(\ensuremath R^s_\lambda f\bigr)''(v) &= 2\lambda \sum_{k=1}^n w_k\,\frac{1}{\ensuremath\sqrt{2\lambda} + \gamma\lambda}\, \int_0^\infty e^{-\ensuremath\sqrt{2\lambda} x}\bigl(f_k(x)-f_k(0)\bigr)\,dx\\ &= \frac{1}{\ensuremath\sqrt{2\lambda}+\gamma\lambda}\,\bigl(2\lambda\,(e^w_\lambda,f) - \ensuremath\sqrt{2\lambda} f(v)\bigr). \qedhere \end{align*} \end{proof} From the identity $A^s \ensuremath R^s_\lambda = \lambda\,\ensuremath R^s_\lambda -\text{id}$ and some simple algebra we get the \begin{corollary} Let $\lambda>0$, and $f\in\ensuremath C_0(\mathcal{G})$. Then \begin{equation} \ensuremath R^s_\lambda f(v) = \frac{1}{\ensuremath\sqrt{2\lambda}+\gamma\lambda}\,\bigl(2\,(e^w_\lambda,f)+\gamma f(v)\bigr) \end{equation} holds. \end{corollary} Since formula~\eqref{eq1.24} in corollary~\ref{cor1.5} is valid for the resolvent of every Brownian motion on $\mathcal{G}$, we may use that formula for $\ensuremath R^s_\lambda f$, sum it against the weights $w_k$, $\ensuremath k=1,\dotsc,n$, and insert the right hand side of equation~\eqref{eq4.11}. This results in \begin{equation*} \sum_{k=1}^n w_k \bigl(\ensuremath R^s_\lambda f\bigr)'(v_k) = \gamma\,\frac{1}{\ensuremath\sqrt{2\lambda}+\gamma\lambda}\,\bigl(2\lambda\,(e^w_\lambda,f)-\ensuremath\sqrt{2\lambda} f(v)\bigr), \end{equation*} and a comparison with formula~\eqref{eq4.8} shows that equation~\eqref{eq4.7} holds true for $f$ replaced by $\ensuremath R^s_\lambda f$ for arbitrary $f\in\ensuremath C_0(\mathcal{G})$. As promised we thus have another proof of theorem~\ref{thm4.2}.

nodes.name: Quantum scattering interpretation of the sticky vertex
nodes.statement: When all $w_m$, $m=1$, \dots, $n$, are equal to $1/n$, the matrix $S^s(\lambda)$ takes the form \begin{equation*} S^s(\lambda) = -1 + \frac{2\ensuremath\sqrt{2\lambda}}{\ensuremath\sqrt{2\lambda} + \gamma \lambda}\,P_n \end{equation*} which reduces to~\eqref{eq2.6a} when $\gamma=0$. $S^s(\lambda)$ is unitary for all $\lambda<0$. Also the $S^s(\lambda)$ for different $\lambda$ all commute. As a consequence $S^s(\lambda)$ has the interpretation of a quantum scattering matrix in the sense of~\cite{KoSc99}. More precisely, $S^s(\lambda)$ stems from the Schr\"odinger operator $-\Delta^s$, where $\Delta^s$ is a self-adjoint Laplace operator on $L^2(\mathcal{G})$ with boundary conditions of the form~\eqref{bc} with the choice \begin{equation} \begin{split} A &= - \frac{1}{2}\,\bigl(S^s(\lambda_0)+1\bigr),\\ B &= - \frac{1}{2\sqrt{\mathstrut2\lambda_0}}\,\bigl(S^s(\lambda_0)-1\bigr), \end{split} \end{equation} for any $\lambda_0$ for which $\sqrt{2\lambda_0}+\gamma\lambda_0\ne 0$. We emphasize that the Schr\"odinger operator $-\Delta^s$ and the generator $A^s$ of the Walsh process are quite different: Not only do they act on different Banach spaces, but also the functions in the intersection of their domains satisfy different boundary conditions at the vertex $v$. As matter of fact, the integral kernel of the resolvent $(-\Delta^s+2\lambda)^{-1}$ of the Schr\"odinger operator $-\Delta^s$ is given by, see Lemma~4.2 in~\cite{KoSc06}, \begin{equation*} \frac{1}{2}\Bigl(r_\lambda(\xi,\eta) +\sum_{k,m=1}^n e_{\lambda,k}(\xi)\, \ensuremath S^s_{km}(\lambda)\,\frac{1}{\ensuremath\sqrt{2\lambda}}\,e_{\lambda,m}(\eta)\Bigl), \end{equation*} that is --- up to a factor $2$ --- by the right hand side of~\eqref{eq4.14a} \emph{without} the last term. In more detail and with the definition~\eqref{SE} \begin{equation*} S_{A,B}\bigl(E=-2\lambda\bigr) = S^s(\lambda) \end{equation*} holds for all $\lambda>0$. As a function of $k$ ($k^2=E$), $S^s$ is meromorphic in the complex $k$--plane with a pole on the positive imaginary axis at $k^b=2i/\gamma$. This corresponds to a negative eigenvalue $E^b=-4/\gamma^2$ of $-\Delta^s$. The corresponding (normalized) eigenfunction $\psi^b$ --- physically speaking a \emph{bound state} --- is given as \begin{equation*} \psi^b(\xi) = \frac{1}{2}\,\sqrt{\frac{\gamma}{n}}\,e^{-2 d(v,\xi)/\gamma},\qquad \xi\in\mathcal{G}. \end{equation*} So quantum mechanically the vertex $v$ acts like an attractive potential. We view this as a quantum analogue of the stickiness of the vertex $v$. This analogy can be elaborated a bit further by inspecting the associated quantum mechanical time delay matrix (see, e.g., \cite{AmJa77, BrFr02, JaMi72, Ma76, Ma81, Na80, Wi55}) \begin{equation*} T(k) = \frac{1}{2ik}\,S(k)^{-1}\frac{\partial}{\partial k} S(k) \end{equation*} which in the present context gives \begin{equation*} T(k) = \frac{-2\gamma}{k(4+k^2\gamma^2)}\,P_n. \end{equation*} So $T(k)$ has zero as an $(n-1)$--fold eigenvalue plus the non-degenerate eigenvalue \begin{equation*} \frac{-2\gamma}{k(4+k^2\gamma^2)}, \end{equation*} which for $\gamma>0$ is the signal for a strict quantum delay. Observe that for $k\to +\infty$, that is for large energies, the time delay experienced by the quantum particle tends to zero, while for $k\to 0$, i.e., for low energies, the delay becomes arbitrarily large. From the physical point of view, both effects are clearly to be expected. For comparison and in contrast to the present stochastic context, in quantum mechanics $\gamma<0$ is also allowed for a meaningful Schr\"odinger operator and an associated scattering matrix.

Let $A^g$ be the generator of $\ensuremath W^g$ with domain $\mathcal{D}(A^g)$. Since $\ensuremath W^g$ is a Brownian motion on $\mathcal{G}$ in the sense of definition~\ref{def_BM}, it follows from theorem~\ref{thm_Feller} that $\mathcal{D}(A^g)\subset \ensuremath C_0^2(\mathcal{G})$, and that for all $f\in\mathcal{D}(A^g)$, $A^g f(\xi) = 1/2\,f''(\xi)$, $\xi\in\mathcal{G}$. Let $h\in\ensuremath C_0(\mathcal{G})$, $\lambda>0$. Then $\ensuremath R^g_\lambda h\in\mathcal{D}(A^g)$, and therefore we may compute with equation~\eqref{eq5.4} as follows \begin{align*} \frac{\gamma}{2}\,\bigl(\ensuremath R^g_\lambda h\bigr)''(v) &= \frac{\gamma}{2}\,\bigl(\ensuremath R^s_\lambda h\bigr)''(v) - \beta\,\rho(\lambda)\,2\lambda \bigl(\ensuremath R^s_\lambda h\bigr)(v)\\ &= \sum_{k=1}^n w_k\,\bigl(\ensuremath R^s_\lambda h\bigr)'(v_k) - \beta\,\rho(\lambda)\,\gamma\lambda \bigl(\ensuremath R^s_\lambda h\bigr)(v), \end{align*} where we used the fact that, since $\ensuremath R^s_\lambda h$ is in the domain of the generator $A^s$ of $\ensuremath W^s$, it satisfies the boundary condition~\eqref{eq4.7}. We rewrite this equation in the following way: \begin{equation} \begin{split} \frac{\gamma}{2}\,\bigl(\ensuremath R^g_\lambda h\bigr)''(v) = \sum_{k=1}^n w_k\,\bigl(\ensuremath R^s_\lambda h\bigr)'(v_k) &+\beta\ensuremath\sqrt{2\lambda}\,\rho(\lambda) \bigl(\ensuremath R^s_\lambda h\bigr)(v)\\ &-\beta\,\rho(\lambda)\bigl(\ensuremath\sqrt{2\lambda}+\gamma\lambda\bigr)\,\bigl(\ensuremath R^s_\lambda h\Bigr)(v). \end{split} \end{equation} Now we differentiate equation~\eqref{eq5.4} at $\xi\in l_k$, $\ensuremath k=1,\dotsc,n$, let $\xi$ tend to $v$ along any edge $l_k$, and sum the resulting equation against the weights $w_k$, $\ensuremath k=1,\dotsc,n$. nodes.section: 5 The General Brownian Motion on a Single Vertex Graph
nodes.label: eq5.14

nodes.name: Transition kernel of W^g (alternative form)
nodes.statement: \begin{split} \ensuremath p^g(t,\xi,d\eta) &= p(t,\xi,\eta)\,d\eta\\ &\hspace{2em} +\sum_{k,m=1}^n \onel(\xi)\,\Bigl(2w_m\,g_{\beta,\gamma}\bigl(t,d_v(\xi,\eta)\bigr)\\ &\hspace{10em} -\delta_{km}\,g\bigl(t,d_v(\xi,\eta)\bigr)\Bigl)\, \onel[m](\eta)\,d\eta\\ &\hspace{2em} + \gamma\,g_{\beta,\gamma}\bigl(t,d(\xi,v)\bigr)\,\epsilon_v(d\eta). \end{split}
nodes.section: 5 The General Brownian Motion on a Single Vertex Graph
nodes.label: eq5.15
